sections.name: Why Hospitals Still Use Leeches

lines.prompt: A Victorian doctor in a top hat holding a large glass jar full of dark leeches up to the light, an apothecary shop behind him

lines: In the 1800s, doctors were so obsessed with leeches that France imported tens of millions of them a year.

lines.prompt: Close-up of a leech attached to a patient's arm in a Victorian clinic, the patient grimacing, gaslight

lines: They put them on almost everything. Headaches, fevers, even bad moods.

lines.prompt: Extreme close-up of a cute but slimy stylized leech's mouth showing a tiny three-part jaw, dark background with soft rim light

lines: A leech has three tiny jaws with rows of teeth, and its spit is full of chemicals that stop blood from clotting.

lines.prompt: Modern operating room, a surgeon in scrubs carefully placing a leech on a patient's reattached finger with tweezers, bright surgical light

lines: And that's why hospitals still use them today. After a surgeon reattaches a finger or an ear, the veins can clog with blood.

lines.prompt: Close-up of a reattached finger with a leech on it, the skin turning from dark purple to healthy pink, clinical lighting

lines: A leech drains the extra blood, and keeps it flowing while the veins heal.

lines.prompt: A modern pharmacy shelf with a sealed medical container of leeches next to regular medicine bottles, a pharmacist smiling

lines: In 2004, the US even approved leeches as an official medical device.
